screens.title: Cisco DNA Center for SD-Access Provisioning
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you'll explore how Cisco DNA Center moves SD-Access from manual CLI tasks into a centrally orchestrated, automated workflow. You'll learn why DNA Center is considered the control plane for provisioning, what it must discover before it can act, and how it maps physical sites into a fabric site for automated role assignment. We'll examine concrete onboarding methods you use to bring switches and routers into inventory, the templates DNA Center applies when you assign Edge, Border, and Control Plane roles, and how IP address pools and virtual networks are tied together so anycast gateways and VTEPs are provisioned consistently. I'll also point out common mistakes — like incorrect CLI or SNMP credentials — that often block deployments, and a few safety practices such as running pre-checks and backups. By the end you'll see how design, provisioning, and assurance in DNA Center reduce repetitive configuration work while keeping the fabric consistent and auditable. Think about one new device you manage today and how DNA Center would discover it, assign a role, and allocate addressing automatically.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These learning objectives map directly to the practical steps you will use in a CCIE-level SD-Access deployment. First, you will learn the role of Cisco DNA Center as the central orchestrator — why it replaces many manual CLI tasks and the specific benefits for consistent VXLAN, LISP, and TrustSec configuration. Second, you will gain working fluency in device onboarding methods: how and when to use IP range discovery, CDP, manual entry, or CSV import and what credentials are required. Third, you will design a network hierarchy and a fabric site, which are essential for applying location-based policies and grouping devices for provisioning. Fourth, you will provision devices into the fabric by assigning Edge, Border, and Control Plane roles, understanding how those roles map to automated configuration templates. Each objective pairs a concrete action with why it matters for operational consistency, reduced errors, and faster rollouts. Throughout, you will also learn common pitfalls to avoid, such as incorrect credentials and global policy risks that can propagate mistakes. Think of these objectives as practical capabilities you can verify in the lab or during an audit of an SD-Access deployment.

screens.title: What is Cisco DNA Center in SD-Access?
screens.narratorSegment: Cisco DNA Center is the central automation and assurance platform used to deploy and operate SD-Access fabrics. At its core, DNA Center translates high-level design choices — like site boundaries, device roles, and virtual networks — into device-level configurations such as VXLAN tunnel endpoints, LISP control plane settings, Anycast gateway assignments, and TrustSec propagation. This orchestration replaces the manual, repetitive work of configuring dozens or hundreds of devices by hand and ensures consistent templates are applied across the fabric. For CCIE-level engineers, understanding CLI remains essential for troubleshooting and deep visibility, but DNA Center shifts regular provisioning tasks into a repeatable GUI-driven workflow. A useful analogy is to think of DNA Center as the compiler for your network intent: you express design intent once, and DNA Center generates the device-specific commands. A common misconception is that DNA Center removes the need to know device behavior; in reality, it amplifies the importance of understanding that generated configuration so you can validate outcomes and troubleshoot when automation encounters exceptions. Key takeaway: DNA Center is both an automation engine and a single source of truth for SD-Access lifecycle operations.

keyIdea.title: Compiler for network intent
keyIdea.text: DNA Center converts design intent into consistent device configurations and provides assurance and inventory to manage SD-Access at scale.

content.html:
Definition
DNA Center as Orchestrator

DNA Center is the platform that centralizes design, provisioning, policy, and assurance for SD-Access. It manages inventory, templates, and automated workflows that produce device-specific configuration.

Analogy
Think of DNA Center as a compiler: high-level intent goes in, device commands come out, and the platform verifies consistency and health.
Misconception
Automation does not negate device knowledge. You must understand the generated configuration to validate or troubleshoot issues.
Key Functions
Inventory & Discovery
Collect devices, credentials, and connectivity.
Design & Sites
Map physical hierarchy to logical fabric sites.
Provisioning
Assign roles and push VXLAN/LISP/TrustSec configs.
IP Management
Central pools for underlay and overlay addressing.
Assurance
Health and client connectivity insights for the fabric.
Templates
Repeatable configuration templates for roles.
Key Takeaway

DNA Center is the single control plane for SD-Access design and provisioning; it reduces manual steps while requiring operator validation and device knowledge.

screens.title: Device Onboarding Methods
screens.narratorSegment: Onboarding devices into DNA Center is the essential first step; without inventory the fabric cannot be provisioned. There are four practical methods: IP Address Range discovery, CDP discovery, manual entry, and CSV import. Use IP range scanning when devices share a predictable management subnet and you want DNA Center to probe many addresses automatically. CDP discovery is useful when a management device has CDP visibility to neighbors and you want DNA Center to find connected devices from a seed list. Manual entry is appropriate for one-off devices or when discovery is restricted by security policies. CSV import is the best choice for bulk onboarding when you have many devices and a prepared dataset. During discovery DNA Center collects management IP, device type, and credentials such as SNMP and CLI. Common errors come from incorrect or expired credentials; if DNA Center cannot authenticate, devices end up in an unmanaged state. A recommended practice is to validate SSH and SNMP credentials on a test device before running a large import. Example: for a 10.1.1.0/24 management network, scanning that range with correct credentials will quickly populate inventory; if you see failures, re-run discovery with verified credentials. After successful onboarding verify device reachability and saved credentials before proceeding to design and provisioning.

keyIdea.title: Choose the right discovery
keyIdea.text: Select IP range for broad scans, CDP for neighbor-based discovery, manual for single devices, and CSV for bulk imports; always verify credentials first.

content.html:
Onboarding Methods
IP Address Range Discovery
Scan a management subnet to discover devices automatically when addresses are known.
CDP Discovery
Seed discovery from a known device using CDP adjacency to find neighbors and expand inventory.
Manual Entry
Add single devices by IP when discovery is not allowed or for isolated devices.
CSV Import
Bulk import devices from a CSV file when onboarding many devices; prepare credentials in advance.
CSV Example
hostname,management_ip,device_type,cli_username,cli_password,snmp_community
DeviceA,10.1.1.10,catalyst9300,admin,Cisco123!,public
DeviceB,10.1.1.11,catalyst9300,admin,Cisco123!,public
Verification & Troubleshooting
  • Always verify SSH and SNMP credentials on a single device before bulk operations to avoid mass failures.
  • If devices appear as "unmanaged", re-run discovery with corrected credentials and confirm IP reachability.
  • Use CDP discovery when devices are reachable through a seed neighbor rather than via wide network scans.
  • For CSV imports, ensure column names match DNA Center expectations and passwords are correct.
Key Takeaway

Pick the discovery method that fits your operational constraints and always validate credentials to avoid unmanaged devices.

screens.title: Credentials, Inventory, and Common Onboarding Mistakes
screens.narratorSegment: When DNA Center discovers a device it must successfully authenticate to collect configuration and manage the device. The platform typically uses SNMP for read/polling, CLI (SSH) for configuration pushes, and HTTP/HTTPS for some A P I-based communications. If any credential is wrong or expired, onboarding can stall: devices may appear in inventory but remain unmanaged or fail during provisioning. A frequent error is using an SNMP community string that is read-only or mismatched between management tools. Another is providing a CLI account without the necessary privilege level to execute configuration commands. To avoid these issues, validate credentials on one device manually: test SSH connectivity, confirm the CLI account can enter configuration mode, and verify SNMP polling returns expected MIB values. In secure environments, management access may be restricted by ACLs; confirm DNA Center's management interface can reach the device IP. Also remember that password policies or account expiry will cause future failures — use service accounts with stable credentials for automation. Finally, document credential sets and map them to device groups so bulk operations use the correct credentials automatically. Credentials, Inventory, and Common Onboarding Mistakes means correct, stable privileges for cli and valid snmp communities are required for successful discovery, provisioning, and ongoing assurance.. In practical terms, why snmp, cli, and http/https credentials matter and how to validate them. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Credentials are foundational
keyIdea.text: Correct, stable privileges for CLI and valid SNMP communities are required for successful discovery, provisioning, and ongoing assurance.

content.html:
Inventory Essentials
Credential types DNA Center needs
  • SNMP - for polling device state and basic inventory data.
  • CLI (SSH) - for pushing configuration and running pre-check commands.
  • HTTP/HTTPS - used by some devices for additional API access where supported.
Validation Steps
Test SSH login and confirm the account can enter configuration mode.
Verify SNMP community strings return expected MIBs with a polling tool.
Confirm DNA Center management IP can reach device IP and that no ACL blocks management traffic.
Common Mistakes
  1. Using expired or single-user accounts that later lock out automation jobs.
  2. Assigning CLI accounts without appropriate privilege levels to push required changes.
  3. CSV imports with incorrect field names or mismatched device types causing discovery errors.
  4. Assuming discovery will work across segmented management networks without verifying connectivity.
Pro Tip

Use service accounts with stable passwords and document their scope. Group devices by credential set to simplify bulk imports.

screens.title: Network Hierarchy and Fabric Site Design
screens.narratorSegment: Designing a network hierarchy in DNA Center is about creating a logical model of your physical deployment that supports location-based policy, assurance, and provisioning. Typical hierarchy levels include Campus, Building, and Floor. You create these sites first under Design > Network Hierarchy and then associate a fabric site to a specific site in that hierarchy. The fabric site defines the boundary where SD-Access will be applied and contains the devices that will participate in the fabric. Within the fabric design you choose which devices will be Fabric Edge Nodes, Fabric Border Nodes, and Control Plane Nodes. A common pattern is to place edge nodes at access-layer switches serving endpoints, border nodes at the site perimeter to hand off external traffic, and control plane nodes in resilient locations to host Map-Server/Map-Resolver functions. The hierarchy matters because policies and VNs can be applied per site or subsite, simplifying segmentation and assurance. A practical tip is to mirror physical cabling and management reachability in the hierarchy so that provisioning operations map naturally to the network topology. Misconfiguring site boundaries can cause incorrect policy scope or provisioning failures, so validate site-device associations before deploying changes.

keyIdea.title: Map physical to logical
keyIdea.text: Create campus/building/floor sites and associate a fabric site so policies and provisioning target the correct set of devices.

content.html:
Hierarchy
Campus > Building > Floor
Create a logical model that reflects physical locations and management reachability so site-scoped policies and provisioning target intended devices.
Site Association
Associate devices to sites before adding them to a fabric to keep policy scope predictable.
Fabric Site
A fabric site defines boundaries for SD-Access and the devices participating in the fabric.
Device Placement Tip
Place control plane nodes in resilient locations and edge nodes at access switches closest to endpoints.
Annotated Site Cards
Campus
Top-level grouping for all buildings and site-wide policies.
Building A
Map specific devices and floors that belong to this building.
Floor 2
Fine-grained site level used for localized policies and assurance.
Check Before Deploy

Confirm device-to-site mapping is accurate to prevent policy scope errors and unexpected provisioning behavior.

screens.title: Designing a Fabric Site and Assigning Roles
screens.narratorSegment: A fabric site in DNA Center groups the devices that will participate in SD-Access and assigns roles that determine the configuration pushed to each device. Fabric Edge Nodes are typically access-layer switches that host endpoint connections and Anycast gateway functions for Virtual Networks. Border Nodes sit at the perimeter and handle external routing, VRF handoffs, and interactions with non-fabric networks. Control Plane Nodes implement the LISP Map-Server and Map-Resolver functionality and maintain the EID-to-RLOC mappings that allow overlay reachability. When designing the fabric, choose Edge devices where hosts attach so Anycast gateways are distributed; place Border devices where handoffs to WAN or data center routers occur; and deploy Control Plane nodes on resilient, redundant hosts. DNA Center provides guided workflows and templates: once you select devices and assign roles, it generates VXLAN VTEP interfaces, LISP configuration, TrustSec settings, and Anycast gateway assignments as needed. A misconception is that role assignment alone completes deployment; in reality you must also associate IP pools and Virtual Networks to ensure address allocation and gateway behavior are correct. Validate role assignments with DNA Center pre-checks before clicking deploy.

keyIdea.title: Roles determine configuration
keyIdea.text: Assigning Edge, Border, and Control Plane roles instructs DNA Center which templates and configurations to push to each device.

content.html:
Role Assignment
Fabric Edge Node
Hosts endpoints, runs Anycast gateway for VNs, and terminates VXLAN VTEP interfaces.
Fabric Border Node
Handles external routing and connectivity to non-fabric networks; often a high-performance router or switch.
Control Plane Node
Implements LISP Map-Server/Map-Resolver functions and maintains EID-to-RLOC mappings for the overlay.
Design Checklist
  • Identify access switches for Edge placement to ensure Anycast gateways are near endpoints.
  • Choose perimeter devices as Border nodes for stable handoff to external routing domains.
  • Deploy two or more Control Plane nodes in resilient locations to host Map-Server/Map-Resolver roles.
  • Associate Virtual Networks and IP pools with the fabric before deploying templates.
Example Role Assignment

Assign Catalyst 9300 switches as Fabric Edge (DeviceA, DeviceB), Catalyst 9300 as second Edge (DeviceC), and Catalyst 9500 as Control Plane or Border depending on external routing needs. Validate with pre-checks.

screens.title: Provisioning Devices into the Fabric
screens.narratorSegment: Provisioning is where DNA Center's automation applies device-specific configuration generated from the design. The high-level steps are: add a fabric under Provision > Fabric, select a site, add devices from inventory, and assign roles for Control Plane, Border, and Edge. DNA Center then prepares templates that include VXLAN VTEP creation, LISP control plane configuration, TrustSec settings for SGT propagation, Anycast gateway addresses for each VN, and necessary underlay addressing. When you click Deploy, DNA Center runs a pre-check to identify connectivity or configuration conflicts, then pushes changes via SSH or A P I to each device. The platform records the deployment and makes the devices available for Assurance. A concrete example: when you assign an Edge node and associate a Virtual Network with a VN address pool, DNA Center will allocate an Anycast gateway IP from that pool and configure the VTEP interface on the Edge node. A common misconception is that provisioning is instantaneous and error-free; always review pre-check output and be prepared to rollback or update templates if a device lacks required privileges. Use small, staged deployments to validate templates before scaling to many sites.

keyIdea.title: Deploy with pre-checks
keyIdea.text: Provisioning assigns templates and pushes configurations, but run pre-checks and stage deployments to detect conflicts before wide changes.

content.html:
Provisioning Steps
  1. Design > Network Hierarchy: confirm site exists.
  2. Design > Network Settings > IP Address Pools: create underlay and overlay pools.
  3. Provision > Fabric: Click Add Fabric and select site.
  4. Add devices and assign Control Plane, Border, Edge roles.
  5. Define VNs and associate IP pools, then Deploy with a Pre-check.
Practical Tip

Stage deployments in a lab or small site first to validate templates and role behavior before site-wide pushes.

What DNA Center Pushes
LISP Control Plane
Map-Server/Map-Resolver roles configured on Control Plane nodes.
VXLAN VTEPs
Tunnel interfaces and VNI mappings on Edge nodes.
TrustSec
SGT propagation and relevant TrustSec configuration.
Anycast Gateways
Anycast IPs allocated from VN pools and configured on Edge nodes.
Key Takeaway

Provisioning automates complex configurations, but pre-checks and staged validation are essential to avoid fabric-wide propagation of errors.

screens.title: What DNA Center Configures Automatically
screens.narratorSegment: When you provision a fabric, DNA Center generates many device-level configurations that are tedious to create manually. The primary items it configures automatically include the LISP control plane, VXLAN VTEP interfaces, Anycast gateway addresses for Virtual Networks, TrustSec SGT propagation, and underlay addressing for loopbacks and p2p links. It will also integrate with ISE for policy enforcement if ISE is in the design. To contrast, tasks you still need to consider manually include some external routing specifics on Border nodes and any vendor- or model-specific tuning not covered by the template. A helpful way to think about this is to divide configuration into overlay, underlay, and integration. Overlay elements like VXLAN VTEPs and Anycast gateways are template-driven; underlay loopbacks and link IPs are allocated from configured pools; integrations such as ISE require correct service configuration on both systems. An important misconception to avoid is believing DNA Center writes every possible setting perfectly for all environments; templates assume typical deployments, so validate generated config and adjust templates when your topology has non-standard features. The concrete practice is to review the planned configuration from DNA Center's GUI before deployment and run a pre-check to capture issues early.

narration.text: When you provision a fabric, DNA Center generates many device-level configurations that are tedious to create manually. screens.title: IP Address Pool Management and Virtual Networks
screens.narratorSegment: IP address pool management in DNA Center is critical because SD-Access automates the allocation of many addresses across the fabric. You define separate pools for the underlay — such as loopbacks used for control plane and point-to-point link addresses — and for the overlay, where Virtual Networks require Anycast gateway subnets. When creating a Virtual Network in Design > Network Settings you associate it with a specific IP address pool so DNA Center can allocate an Anycast gateway IP to each Fabric Edge node that participates in that VN. This prevents manual errors and address conflicts. DNA Center can also manage DHCP services for overlay subnets if configured. A concrete example: create an overlay pool named VN_Users with subnet 10.10.10.0/24 and associate it to the 'Users' VN; DNA Center will allocate gateway addresses across Edge nodes from that pool. Misconception: do not assume pools are unlimited; carefully plan pool sizes to accommodate the number of sites and required subnets. Regularly review pools and reclaim unused ranges to keep addressing predictable across the fabric. screens.title: GUI Workflow: A Simplified Provisioning Walkthrough
screens.narratorSegment: A typical GUI workflow in DNA Center for provisioning a fabric follows a predictable sequence that you should memorize. First, in Design > Network Hierarchy create or confirm your Campus, Building, and Floor sites so your fabric can be associated with a clear boundary. Second, under Design > Network Settings > IP Address Pools define underlay pools for loopbacks and point-to-point links and overlay pools for Virtual Networks. Third, go to Provision > Fabric and click Add Fabric, selecting the site you prepared. Fourth, add devices from inventory and assign their roles: Control Plane, Border, and Edge. Fifth, define Virtual Networks and associate them with the overlay pools you created. Sixth, run the Pre-check that DNA Center provides; address any warnings or errors, then click Deploy to push configuration. After deployment, use Assurance to monitor fabric health and client connectivity. The reason this sequence matters is that IP pools and site topology must exist before role assignment so allocated addresses and Anycast gateways are correctly computed. Practice this sequence in the lab mentally or with a mock GUI to build muscle memory and avoid ordering mistakes.

screens.title: Safety Notes, Assurance, and Troubleshooting Provisioning Failures
screens.narratorSegment: DNA Center includes several safety mechanisms but operators must use them. Before deploying any fabric changes run the DNA Center pre-check to surface connectivity, credential, and template conflicts. Always back up the DNA Center appliance configuration before large changes so you can recover from accidental global updates. Use Assurance to monitor fabric health and client connectivity after deployment and to diagnose issues. A common provisioning failure is the 'device unreachable' error. The most likely initial troubleshooting step is to re-run device discovery and confirm the CLI and SNMP credentials; if credentials are wrong DNA Center cannot establish management connections. Also verify IP reachability and that no access lists or firewall rules block DNA Center management traffic. If pre-checks report missing privileges, ensure the CLI account has the required privilege level to push configuration. When troubleshooting, collect logs and use Assurance to identify whether failures are localized to a device or widespread across the fabric. The practical approach is to iterate: fix credential or connectivity issues, re-run discovery, reassign role if needed, and then re-deploy after a successful pre-check. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you'll explore how Cisco DNA Center moves SD-Access from manual CLI tasks into a centrally orchestrated, automated workflow. You'll learn why DNA Center is considered the control plane for provisioning, what it must discover before it can act, and how it maps physical sites into a fabric site for automated role assignment. We'll examine concrete onboarding methods you use to bring switches and routers into inventory, the templates DNA Center applies when you assign Edge, Border, and Control Plane roles, and how IP address pools and virtual networks are tied together so anycast gateways and VTEPs are provisioned consistently. I'll also point out common mistakes — like incorrect CLI or SNMP credentials — that often block deployments, and a few safety practices such as running pre-checks and backups. By the end you'll see how design, provisioning, and assurance in DNA Center reduce repetitive configuration work while keeping the fabric consistent and auditable. Think about one new device you manage today and how DNA Center would discover it, assign a role, and allocate addressing automatically.

These learning objectives map directly to the practical steps you will use in a CCIE-level SD-Access deployment. First, you will learn the role of Cisco DNA Center as the central orchestrator — why it replaces many manual CLI tasks and the specific benefits for consistent VXLAN, LISP, and TrustSec configuration. Second, you will gain working fluency in device onboarding methods: how and when to use IP range discovery, CDP, manual entry, or CSV import and what credentials are required. Third, you will design a network hierarchy and a fabric site, which are essential for applying location-based policies and grouping devices for provisioning. Fourth, you will provision devices into the fabric by assigning Edge, Border, and Control Plane roles, understanding how those roles map to automated configuration templates. Each objective pairs a concrete action with why it matters for operational consistency, reduced errors, and faster rollouts. Throughout, you will also learn common pitfalls to avoid, such as incorrect credentials and global policy risks that can propagate mistakes. Think of these objectives as practical capabilities you can verify in the lab or during an audit of an SD-Access deployment.

These additional objectives focus on safe, verifiable operations and lab practice you should be able to perform. First, you will learn to prepare devices with correct CLI and SNMP credentials and run discovery methods that collect inventory reliably; this prevents 'unmanaged' states. Second, you will manage IP address pools: create underlay pools for loopbacks and point-to-point links and overlay pools for Virtual Networks so subnets are allocated consistently. Third, you will practice pre-deploy checks and backups: always run DNA Center's pre-check, and ensure the appliance configuration is backed up before global changes. Fourth, you will complete a simulated onboarding and role assignment exercise for small lab topologies so you can reason about role placement and addressing decisions. These skills combine practical lab readiness with operational caution. They matter because an automated platform can scale mistakes as quickly as it scales success, so a disciplined workflow keeps the fabric stable and auditable.

Cisco DNA Center is the central automation and assurance platform used to deploy and operate SD-Access fabrics. At its core, DNA Center translates high-level design choices — like site boundaries, device roles, and virtual networks — into device-level configurations such as VXLAN tunnel endpoints, LISP control plane settings, Anycast gateway assignments, and TrustSec propagation. This orchestration replaces the manual, repetitive work of configuring dozens or hundreds of devices by hand and ensures consistent templates are applied across the fabric. For CCIE-level engineers, understanding CLI remains essential for troubleshooting and deep visibility, but DNA Center shifts regular provisioning tasks into a repeatable GUI-driven workflow. A useful analogy is to think of DNA Center as the compiler for your network intent: you express design intent once, and DNA Center generates the device-specific commands. A common misconception is that DNA Center removes the need to know device behavior; in reality, it amplifies the importance of understanding that generated configuration so you can validate outcomes and troubleshoot when automation encounters exceptions. Key takeaway: DNA Center is both an automation engine and a single source of truth for SD-Access lifecycle operations.

Onboarding devices into DNA Center is the essential first step; without inventory the fabric cannot be provisioned. There are four practical methods: IP Address Range discovery, CDP discovery, manual entry, and CSV import. Use IP range scanning when devices share a predictable management subnet and you want DNA Center to probe many addresses automatically. CDP discovery is useful when a management device has CDP visibility to neighbors and you want DNA Center to find connected devices from a seed list. Manual entry is appropriate for one-off devices or when discovery is restricted by security policies. CSV import is the best choice for bulk onboarding when you have many devices and a prepared dataset. During discovery DNA Center collects management IP, device type, and credentials such as SNMP and CLI. Common errors come from incorrect or expired credentials; if DNA Center cannot authenticate, devices end up in an unmanaged state. A recommended practice is to validate SSH and SNMP credentials on a test device before running a large import. Example: for a 10.1.1.0/24 management network, scanning that range with correct credentials will quickly populate inventory; if you see failures, re-run discovery with verified credentials. After successful onboarding verify device reachability and saved credentials before proceeding to design and provisioning.

When DNA Center discovers a device it must successfully authenticate to collect configuration and manage the device. The platform typically uses SNMP for read/polling, CLI (SSH) for configuration pushes, and HTTP/HTTPS for some A P I-based communications. If any credential is wrong or expired, onboarding can stall: devices may appear in inventory but remain unmanaged or fail during provisioning. A frequent error is using an SNMP community string that is read-only or mismatched between management tools. Another is providing a CLI account without the necessary privilege level to execute configuration commands. To avoid these issues, validate credentials on one device manually: test SSH connectivity, confirm the CLI account can enter configuration mode, and verify SNMP polling returns expected MIB values. In secure environments, management access may be restricted by ACLs; confirm DNA Center's management interface can reach the device IP. Also remember that password policies or account expiry will cause future failures — use service accounts with stable credentials for automation. Finally, document credential sets and map them to device groups so bulk operations use the correct credentials automatically. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Designing a network hierarchy in DNA Center is about creating a logical model of your physical deployment that supports location-based policy, assurance, and provisioning. Typical hierarchy levels include Campus, Building, and Floor. You create these sites first under Design > Network Hierarchy and then associate a fabric site to a specific site in that hierarchy. The fabric site defines the boundary where SD-Access will be applied and contains the devices that will participate in the fabric. Within the fabric design you choose which devices will be Fabric Edge Nodes, Fabric Border Nodes, and Control Plane Nodes. A common pattern is to place edge nodes at access-layer switches serving endpoints, border nodes at the site perimeter to hand off external traffic, and control plane nodes in resilient locations to host Map-Server/Map-Resolver functions. The hierarchy matters because policies and VNs can be applied per site or subsite, simplifying segmentation and assurance. A practical tip is to mirror physical cabling and management reachability in the hierarchy so that provisioning operations map naturally to the network topology. Misconfiguring site boundaries can cause incorrect policy scope or provisioning failures, so validate site-device associations before deploying changes.

A fabric site in DNA Center groups the devices that will participate in SD-Access and assigns roles that determine the configuration pushed to each device. Fabric Edge Nodes are typically access-layer switches that host endpoint connections and Anycast gateway functions for Virtual Networks. Border Nodes sit at the perimeter and handle external routing, VRF handoffs, and interactions with non-fabric networks. Control Plane Nodes implement the LISP Map-Server and Map-Resolver functionality and maintain the EID-to-RLOC mappings that allow overlay reachability. When designing the fabric, choose Edge devices where hosts attach so Anycast gateways are distributed; place Border devices where handoffs to WAN or data center routers occur; and deploy Control Plane nodes on resilient, redundant hosts. DNA Center provides guided workflows and templates: once you select devices and assign roles, it generates VXLAN VTEP interfaces, LISP configuration, TrustSec settings, and Anycast gateway assignments as needed. A misconception is that role assignment alone completes deployment; in reality you must also associate IP pools and Virtual Networks to ensure address allocation and gateway behavior are correct. Validate role assignments with DNA Center pre-checks before clicking deploy.

Provisioning is where DNA Center's automation applies device-specific configuration generated from the design. The high-level steps are: add a fabric under Provision > Fabric, select a site, add devices from inventory, and assign roles for Control Plane, Border, and Edge. DNA Center then prepares templates that include VXLAN VTEP creation, LISP control plane configuration, TrustSec settings for SGT propagation, Anycast gateway addresses for each VN, and necessary underlay addressing. When you click Deploy, DNA Center runs a pre-check to identify connectivity or configuration conflicts, then pushes changes via SSH or A P I to each device. The platform records the deployment and makes the devices available for Assurance. A concrete example: when you assign an Edge node and associate a Virtual Network with a VN address pool, DNA Center will allocate an Anycast gateway IP from that pool and configure the VTEP interface on the Edge node. A common misconception is that provisioning is instantaneous and error-free; always review pre-check output and be prepared to rollback or update templates if a device lacks required privileges. Use small, staged deployments to validate templates before scaling to many sites.
